---
name: theme-an-app
description: Give a SwiftUI iPhone or iPad app its own fonts and colours, light and dark, from one theme document, using the RipulAgent Swift package. Use when asked to theme, brand or restyle an app, to make an app follow a website's or a brand's look, to adapt an app's source to theme tokens, or to say what a theme would reach in an app.
---

# Giving an app a theme

A theme here is one JSON document: colours for light and dark, three font families, and sizes and weights. The RipulAgent Swift package reads it and the app's own screens follow it. This is the procedure for doing that in someone's repository. Follow it in order. It needs RipulAgent 0.7.172 or later.

Three rules hold throughout:

- **With no theme document the app must look exactly as it did.** Every step below keeps that, and you prove it with screenshots before you call the work done.
- **Start with the level that changes no source.** Go further only where the person asks for more.
- **The tools read text, not Swift.** What they write and what they count is a draft. A build and a screenshot are the proof.

## 1. Find out what the app is

Read the repository's instructions for agents and its project files before anything else. You need to know:

- **Is it a SwiftUI app for iOS?** This works for a SwiftUI app with a deployment target of iOS 17 or later. If the repository is something else (a website, an Android app, a server, a React Native or Flutter app), say so plainly and stop: nothing here applies. A UIKit app can read the theme through `UIColor.ripul(…)` and `UIFont.ripul(…)` by hand, and gets nothing from levels 1 and 3; say that and ask before going on.
- **How it is built**: an XcodeGen `project.yml`, a hand-kept `.xcodeproj`, or a Swift package; the scheme; where build output goes; which Xcode.
- **Does it link the package already**, and at which version? Look for `ripul-ios-sdk` in `project.yml`, `Package.swift` or `Package.resolved`.
- **How a screen is opened without tapping**: launch arguments, deep links, previews. You will need this for screenshots.

If the person asked only what a theme would reach, do step 3 and stop: change nothing and report.

## 2. Work on a branch

Never on the default branch. Make a branch from it (`git switch -c theme`). If the working tree has changes you did not make, say so and ask before going on. Commit as you go, so each level can be kept or dropped by itself.

## 3. Measure before you touch anything

**Get the tools.** They are in the package, in `tools/`, and need only `python3`. Where the app links the package they are in its checkout: `<derived data>/SourcePackages/checkouts/ripul-ios-sdk/tools/ripul-theme` in an Xcode project, `.build/checkouts/ripul-ios-sdk/tools/ripul-theme` in a Swift package. Where it does not yet, or to look without building: `git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/ripulio/ripul-ios-sdk /tmp/ripul-ios-sdk`.

**Count what a theme would reach.** Neither command changes a file:

```bash
ripul-theme check <source folder>                      # every font and colour written at a call site, by kind
ripul-theme migrate --dry-run --named <source folder>  # the lines level 3 would rewrite
```

   In a hand-kept Xcode project it is the target's Build Phases, "Run Build Tool Plug-ins": ask the person to add it there, since a project file edited by hand is easy to break. In a Swift package it is `plugins: [.plugin(name: "RipulThemeRedirect", package: "ripul-ios-sdk")]` on the target (this compiles; it has not been run in a real package host).
3. **Allow the plug-in to run.** Xcode refuses a package's plug-in until it is trusted, and the build fails with the one line `Validate plug-in “RipulThemeRedirect” in package “ripul-ios-sdk”`. On the command line add `-skipPackagePluginValidation` to every `xcodebuild` call, and add it to the repository's build scripts and written commands too, or the next agent meets the same failure. In Xcode itself the person is asked once, "Trust & Enable".
4. **Build with no theme document yet**, and take the screenshots again. Compare them with the baseline pixel for pixel, by decoding both and counting the pixels that differ, never by eye. They must match, apart from the screens your two baseline sets showed to differ by themselves. If the build fails with "invalid redeclaration" or "ambiguous use", the app declares a name the generated file also declares; the header of the generated file names two flags that leave a part out (`RIPUL_THEME_NO_ROOT`, `RIPUL_THEME_NO_STYLES`). `docs/theming-for-hosts.md` in the package checkout, "What can go wrong", has the rest.

## 5. Write the theme document

Ask what the look should follow if the person has not said: a website, a brand file, a design. Then take the values from it; do not invent a palette.

- **From a website:** fetch its stylesheets and read the page background, the text colour, the accent (links and buttons), the card and panel colours, and the font families for headings and for text. Report the values you took and where each came from.
- **Write `<name>.json`** in a folder the app bundles (the bundle's top level, or a folder named `Theme` or `Themes`). The keys, the fifteen colour roles and what each is for are in `docs/theming-for-hosts.md`, "Write the document". Start from `{ "schema": 1, "name": "…" }`, which changes nothing, and add to it.
- **Light and dark are both yours to write.** A source that has only a light look gives you no dark values: derive them, say that you derived them, and check each dark text colour against its background yourself. Nothing checks contrast. The pair most often wrong is `onAccent` on a pale dark-mode accent.
- **With one theme document in the bundle, it is the app's theme** at the next launch. With more than one, name one with the Info.plist key `RipulTheme`, or the app stays on the system look and says so in its log.

**Fonts.** A font may be bundled only if its licence allows embedding in an app. Fonts served by Adobe Fonts, and most fonts a foundry sells for the web, do not allow it. When the brand's font cannot be bundled, say so, propose the nearest font that can (the SIL Open Font Licence allows it), and let the person decide. Put the `.ttf` or `.otf` files in the bundle (top level, or a folder named `Fonts`), each font's licence file beside it, and a short note of where each file came from. Write no registration code and no Info.plist entry: the package registers the files a document names. The name in the document is the font's family name ("Source Sans 3"), not its file name. Prefer a variable font: a file with one weight draws that weight whatever is asked.

**Look at it.** Build, and capture the same screens in light and dark. Open the pictures and read them. To see the app without the theme, launch it with `-ripul.theme.document system`; to see another document, pass its name. That argument lasts for one launch.

## 6. Say what level 1 did not reach, and ask

Level 1 reaches: text styles and fixed sizes, a serif or monospaced design, hierarchy styles in `foregroundStyle`, the system background colours, the named state colours (red, orange, green, blue, grey), the accent, navigation titles and tab labels.

It does not reach, and you should name each with the screens where it shows:

- **text with no colour of its own**, which stays the system's black or white on the theme's ground;
- **lists and forms**: their ground, rows and header colour;
- **the app's own colours** (an asset colour, a `Brand` type), and white and black;
- a prominent button's label, a hierarchy style given to `fill`, `stroke` or `background`, and UIKit code.

**Stop here and ask.** Show the themed screenshots, list what was not reached, and ask which the person wants: stop at level 1; fix the few places that matter (level 2); or adapt the whole source (level 3). Do not go on unasked.

## 7. Level 2: a few lines where it matters

Each is a small edit in the app's source, in a file that imports `RipulAgent`. The forms are in `docs/theming-for-hosts.md`, "What it leaves for you". The three that matter most:

- **A text colour:** `.foregroundStyle(.ripul(.text))` on the `Text` itself. Never on a container or the root: there it recolours the labels of buttons, list links and section headers.
- **A list:** `.scrollContentBackground(.hidden)` and `.background(.ripul(.surfaceSunken))` on the list, and `.listRowBackground(Color.ripul(.surface))` on each section or row. On the list itself the row background does nothing.
- **The app's own colour:** ask. Either it stays fixed, or it gives way to the theme: `RipulTheme.isDefault(.accent) ? myNavy : Color.ripul(.accent)`, read where it is used. A theme document cannot name a colour outside the fifteen roles.

## 8. Level 3: adapt the source

Only when asked. It rewrites call sites to explicit accessors (`.font(.ripul(.body))`), so the source says it is themed and a check can keep it so. The two levels mix a file at a time: a migrated file calls the accessors, and the rest still goes through the plug-in.

```bash
ripul-theme migrate --dry-run --named <source folder>   # read this first
ripul-theme migrate --named <source folder>
ripul-theme check <source folder>                       # what is left; exit 1 while any is
ripul-theme lint                                        # did each replacement keep its value?
```

What the tool does not do, each measured on a real app:

- **It adds no `import RipulAgent`.** Every file it rewrote needs one, or one `@_exported import RipulAgent` in the app's main file.
- **It does not follow the app's own font helper** (`static func serif(…) -> Font`), and with `--named` it leaves `.black.opacity(…)` inside a gradient or a shadow. `check` lists each.
- **`lint` reports a line you added by hand** (a root line, a list modifier) as "the hunk adds and removes different numbers of lines". That is the lint not knowing the line, not a moved value.
- **A zero from `check` is not proof.** It cannot see a bare `.orange` passed to an unlabelled parameter, or a new `Text` with no colour.

Finish what `check` lists by the tables in `docs/theming-for-hosts.md` ("Move the call sites" and "What it leaves for you"). A colour that is data (a category's, a chart's, a shade over a photo) takes `// theme-exempt: <reason>` on its line and stays.

## 9. Prove nothing moved

After the last edit, whatever the level:

1. Launch with `-ripul.theme.document system` (or with no theme document in the bundle) and capture every baseline screen again, light and dark.
2. Compare with the baseline pixel for pixel. A screen that differs must be one that differed between your two baseline sets, in the same place. Anything else is an edit that changed the app: find it and fix it.
3. After level 3, `lint` must have nothing to say about a line the tool wrote.
4. Build Release once. The View Explorer's map is left out of it, and the theme must still load.

## 10. Hand back a ledger

Do not merge. Report, with each line marked measured or reasoned:

- the branch, and what `git diff --shortstat <default branch>` reads; how many Swift lines changed (none, after level 1);
- the files added: the document, each font with its licence and where it came from, any stand-in for a font that could not be bundled;
- every build command and script that gained `-skipPackagePluginValidation`;
- what follows the theme and what does not, by kind, with a screenshot for each;
- the comparison: how many screens, how many the same, and why each of the others differs;
- every decision you made for the person and every one still open (the app's own colours, dark values you derived, a font you substituted);
- what you did not test: a phone, Dynamic Type, Increased Contrast, right-to-left, an archive.

## Limits to say out loud

- Level 1 rests on how the Swift compiler chooses between two declarations of one name, measured with Swift 6.4 and Xcode 27.1 and not promised by the language. If a compiler changes it, the likely result is a compile error in the app's files, and the cure is to switch the plug-in off.
- The theme is part of the whole package: an app that wants only the theme links all of it, in Release too.
- A theme document cannot add a colour role, ask for a font feature such as lining figures, or colour a large navigation title or a section header.
- If you are running inside Ripul (you have a `ripul_guide` tool), read its `devices` and `trains` guides before you install a build on a phone or use a simulator another agent may hold.

# Shipping skills, not only guides

A proposal, 11 October 2026. Nothing here is built except where "What exists today" says so. Each fact is marked **checked** (read in the code or run on the Mac Studio) or **reasoned**.

## Recommendation

**Keep one text per skill, and let the host hand it to each agent at launch, from a folder the host owns. Start with Claude, where it is one argument.**

1. **A skill is a guide with a heading block.** Write each as `SKILL.md` (a name, a one-sentence description of when to use it, then the procedure). The guide that `ripul_guide` serves is the same file without the heading block. This is how the theming skill ships today, with a build check that the two cannot drift.
2. **The host keeps the skills in its own folder** (`~/.ripul/skills/`), fetched from the web deploy the way guides are, so a new skill needs a web deploy and no new host build.
3. **Claude gets the folder as a plug-in for that session**: one more launch argument, `--plugin-dir`. Nothing is written into the person's repository or into their own Claude settings. The skills appear in the agent's own list, named `ripul:<skill>`.
4. **Codex and Antigravity come second**, each after one test (below). Until then they keep the guide, which already reaches all three.
5. **For a person who does not use Ripul**, a skill ships inside the thing it is about, with one command to install it. The SDK does this today for theming.

Cost, reasoned from the size of the code: step 3 is about half a day with its tests. Step 2 is about a day. I would do 3 first with the folder filled at build time, and 2 after.

## Problem

Ripul ships product knowledge to agents as guides. A guide is read only when the agent is pointed at it: by the one-paragraph harness note, by the list in the `ripul_guide` tool's description, or by a starting prompt that names it. An agent that is asked "give this app a theme" in plain words, with no pointer, may never open the guide.

A skill is different in two ways. It sits in the agent's own list with a description, so the agent chooses it by itself when the request matches. And a person can call it by name. Neither is true of a guide.

There is a second audience a guide cannot reach at all: a developer who uses our SDK with Claude Code or Codex and does not run Ripul.

## What exists today

**Guides (checked).** Nine, now ten, Markdown files in `chrome-extension/public/guides/`, listed in `index.json`, fetched by `ripul_guide` with no caching (`RipulGuideHandler.ts`). Live with a web deploy. They reach Claude, Codex and Antigravity alike.

**The harness note (checked, `CliServerBase.swift:29`).** One paragraph telling the agent it is inside Ripul and to call `ripul_guide` before using artefacts, plans, the browser, voice or shared builds. Claude gets it by `--append-system-prompt`. Codex gets it after the person's own developer instructions. Antigravity does not get it.

**What the host passes at launch (checked).**

| | Arguments that matter here | Could carry skills today? |
|---|---|---|
| Claude (`ClaudeCliServer.swift`) | `--mcp-config` with `--strict-mcp-config`, `--append-system-prompt`, `--tools`, the chat's folder as working directory. No `--plugin-dir`, `--add-dir` or `--settings`. Every inherited `CLAUDE_CODE_*` variable is removed. `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` is set to the account profile's folder when there is one. | No. One argument away. |
| Codex (`CodexCliServer.swift`, `CodexSharedProvider.swift`) | `-c` overrides for the tools server, the sandbox and developer instructions; per thread, a `config` object. `CODEX_HOME` is read and never set. | No. |
| Antigravity (`AntigravityCliServer.swift`) | `agy -p … --add-dir <folder>`. The host writes `<folder>/.agents/mcp_config.json` before a turn and removes it after. | No, though it already writes into `.agents/`. |

**How each agent finds a skill (checked by placing a probe skill and reading what the agent listed, except where marked).**

| | Version on this Mac | In a repository | For the person | For one session |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | 2.1.283 | `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | `~/.claude/skills/` | `--plugin-dir <folder>`: the plug-in's skills were listed as `<plugin>:<skill>`. Also `.claude/skills` inside an `--add-dir` folder. |
| Codex | 0.159.3 | `.agents/skills/` and `.codex/skills/`. Not `.claude/skills`. | `~/.codex/skills/` | None found. The binary has a `skills.config` setting with path entries; not tested. |
| Antigravity | not installed here | `.agents/skills/` or `.agent/skills/` (from memory, not checked) | `~/.gemini/antigravity/skills/` (from memory) | Unknown. |

**Instruction files (checked for two).** Claude read `CLAUDE.md` and not `AGENTS.md`. Codex read `AGENTS.md` and not `CLAUDE.md`. Antigravity is from memory: `AGENTS.md` and `GEMINI.md`.

**In Ripul's apps (checked).** Nothing lists, syncs or offers skills. A Claude `Skill` tool call is drawn with an icon and its name; that is all. The slash menu shows the web app's own commands.

**The first skill (built today).** `ripul-ios-sdk/tools/skills/theme-an-app/SKILL.md`, in the public package from 0.7.172. `tools/ripul-theme install-skill <repository>` copies it to `.claude/skills` and `.agents/skills`. The `theming` guide is the same text, and the web build fails if they differ.

## Options

**A. Guides only, with better pointers.** Add each topic to the tool's description and to starting prompts. No new machinery. It still depends on the agent reading a list, the list grows in every session, and it does nothing for a person outside Ripul.

**B. Files in the repository.** The host, or a command, writes `.claude/skills` and `.agents/skills` into the person's repository. Works for all three agents (reasoned for Antigravity). It changes a customer's working tree, shows in `git status`, and goes stale: a copy is as old as the day it was made. Right for a team that wants the skill in their repository, wrong as the default.

**C. A plug-in folder handed to the agent at launch.** The recommendation. Nothing in the repository, nothing in the person's settings, always the current text. Checked for Claude. For Codex it needs a test of `skills.config` passed with `-c`; if that fails, the fallback is the person's `~/.codex/skills/`, which is their folder and needs their consent.

**D. A plug-in marketplace.** Publish a repository of plug-ins (`ripulio/skills`) that a person adds once in Claude Code or Codex; both have a marketplace command (checked that the commands exist, not used). This is the route for people who do not run Ripul, and it would carry more than skills. It is a product decision with a public face, so it is not where to start.

**E. In the package the skill is about.** As the SDK does now. Reaches anyone who has the package, needs a release to change, and needs one command to install. Good for a skill about one package; not a way to ship Ripul's own knowledge.

C and E together cover both audiences. D can follow if skills prove their worth.

## Open questions

1. **Which guides become skills?** A skill's description is in the agent's context in every session, so the list must stay short. My view: the ones a request triggers in plain words (theming, artefacts, plans, the CMS). The ones about how to behave inside Ripul (session, trains, devices) stay guides behind the harness note.
2. **Does Codex take a skills folder for one session?** One test of `-c skills.config=…` settles it. Until then Codex keeps the guide.
3. **Antigravity** is not installed on the Mac Studio. Its part is unverified until it is.
4. **Two copies of one skill.** A person may have installed a skill into their repository and also get it from the host. Claude names the host's `ripul:<skill>`, so both show. Whether that confuses needs looking at once.
5. **Account profiles.** When the host sets `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, the person's own skills come from that folder, not `~/.claude` (reasoned, not tested). Unrelated to shipping ours, but it means a person's skills can vanish in a Ripul chat today.
6. **Should Ripul's slash menu list the agent's skills?** The CLI reports them when a session starts and the host does not read that. It would make "use the theme skill" a tap.
7. **Starting prompts.** Today the theming rows say "read the theming guide from the ripul_guide tool first". With skills they could say less. Worth changing only after C is measured.

3. **Antigravity** is not installed on the Mac Studio. Its part is unverified until it is.
4. **Two copies of one skill.** A person may have installed a skill into their repository and also get it from the host. Claude names the host's `ripul:<skill>`, so both show. Whether that confuses needs looking at once.
5. **Account profiles.** When the host sets `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, the person's own skills come from that folder, not `~/.claude` (reasoned, not tested). Unrelated to shipping ours, but it means a person's skills can vanish in a Ripul chat today.
6. **Should Ripul's slash menu list the agent's skills?** The CLI reports them when a session starts and the host does not read that. It would make "use the theme skill" a tap.
7. **Starting prompts.** Today the theming rows say "read the theming guide from the ripul_guide tool first". With skills they could say less. Worth changing only after C is measured.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Count fonts and colours written at the call site, and refuse a count that rises.

Every font and colour in the first-party apps is moving to a theme token
(docs/plans/theme-aware-codebase.md; what to write instead is in
ripul-ios-sdk/docs/theming.md). This check keeps the tree from refilling
behind the migration, and its totals are the progress measure.

  check_theme_tokens.py                  compare with the baselines (this is what the app build runs)
  check_theme_tokens.py --report         the same, with the table of every stream
  check_theme_tokens.py --paths A B ...  the counted lines in those files or directories, then the comparison
  check_theme_tokens.py --list S1        every counted line in a stream
  check_theme_tokens.py --update S1      lower a stream's baseline to today's counts
  check_theme_tokens.py --finish S1      mark a stream finished (its counts must be zero)

Counted, per line, comments stripped:
  font       .font(.body), Font.system(...), UIFont.systemFont(...) and the like
  colour     Color.red, .foregroundStyle(.orange), UIColor.systemBackground, Color(red:...), .cgColor of those
  hierarchy  .primary/.secondary/.tertiary/.quaternary as a style, Color.primary, Color.secondary
  stored     an accessor's result kept in a `static let`: it would never follow a theme change

Counted apart, never failing: the system form (`.ripul(system: ...)`), and exempt lines.

A bare name (`.orange`, `.secondary`) is counted inside a style call (`foregroundStyle`,
`fill`, `tint` and the rest), in an argument whose label names a colour (`tint: .blue`,
`colors: [.blue, .purple]`), on a line that says its type is `Color`, and after `return`.
A bare text style (`.caption`) is counted anywhere inside a `.font(...)` argument, on a
line that says its type is `Font`, and after `return`.
It cannot see every one: a bare name passed to an unlabelled parameter is invisible to
it, so a count of zero is not proof that a file is clean. Read the diff too.

entries.name: mcp__ripul_tools__await_agent
entries.description:
Wait for a reply to a message you sent (send_to_agent) or a task you started (spawn_agent), and return it. Pass the handle
those calls returned, or an agentId to wait for whatever that agent is doing. timeoutSec 0 checks without waiting.
A handle or agentId from another Mac waits on that Mac, for up to 240 seconds a call.

agentId.description: Wait on this agent instead (uses your latest message to it, else its current turn).

handle.description: The handle returned by send_to_agent or spawn_agent.

timeoutSec.description: How long to wait (default 240, max 280). 0 = check and return immediately.

entries.name: mcp__ripul_tools__list_agents
entries.description:
List the other agent sessions on this machine (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity): which are running now or ran recently,
what each is working on, its model, working directory and branch, and the device each works on (its working device,
and whether it holds it). Also lists the CLIs available for spawn_agent and any messages you have in flight. Use the
returned agentId with send_to_agent and await_agent.
The result names the other Macs of this account under machines. Pass machine: "all" for every Mac at once, in one
list that says which machine each agent is on and what each Mac can start; a Mac that does not answer is named and
the rest are still listed. Pass a machine's name for that one alone. An agentId from another Mac names that Mac and
works as it is.

machine.description: List another Mac of this account instead of this one, by its name (e.g. Macbook) or machineId, or "all" for every Mac at once.

sinceHours.description: How far back "recent" reaches, in hours (default 24).

status.description: running = only agents mid-turn; recent (default) = running or active within sinceHours; all = everything on disk.

entries.name: mcp__ripul_tools__spawn_agent
entries.description:
Start a new agent session on this machine to work on a task, in a new chat of its own that the user can open. Choose the
CLI with harness (claude, codex, antigravity) or model, or leave harness as auto to pick by task: Codex for well-specified
code changes (implementing, refactors, tests, build errors), Claude for design, review, investigation and writing. The
agent's final reply comes back to you like a send_to_agent reply. Returns its agentId and a handle for await_agent.
To start an agent "on" a phone (for example to run tests on the iPhone 16), pass device: the agent still runs on this
Mac, but that phone becomes its working device, where its device_* tools act, and it holds the phone so other agents
can't use it at the same time. It hands the phone back when archived, when it moves, or after an hour without using it.
To start it on another Mac of this account, pass machine. That Mac chooses the CLI, checks the model against what it
has (its local models too: see list_agents with machine) and counts the agent against its own limit, so work can go
to the Mac with the model or the spare capacity. The reply still comes back to you.

device.description: The phone or other device to put the agent on: a handle from device_list_targets (e.g. iphone-c603) or a model name that matches one connected device (e.g. "iPhone 16 Pro Max"). Refused if another agent holds it.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for the new session (default the CLI's own).

expectReply.description: Whether its final reply should come back to you (default true).

harness.description: Which CLI to run it in (default auto). The result says which was picked and why.

machine.description: Start the agent on another Mac of this account: its name (e.g. Macbook) or machineId, from list_agents. Without cwd it starts in the same repository on that Mac when that Mac has it, else in that Mac's default folder. harness, model and device are then that Mac's.

model.description: Exact model id, overriding harness (e.g. claude-cli-raw-opus, claude-cli-raw-sonnet, codex-shared-cli-raw-default).

task.description: The complete task. The new agent starts with no context but this and its working directory.

timeoutSec.description: With wait, how long to wait (default 240, max 280).

title.description: Chat title (default the first line of the task).

wait.description: Wait for its first reply and return it (default false).

}ripul-train — ask Trainyard to ship something, hold a resource, hold back a
commit, or see what is going on. Run it from anywhere inside the repository.

  ripul-train request <track> [--wait] [--checked] [--sha <commit>] [--pull] [-- <job args>]
                                     --pull: in-place tracks fast-forward to the branch first
  ripul-train hold <resource> --reason "…" [--ttl <minutes>]
  ripul-train release <holdId|leaseId>
  ripul-train acquire <pool> [key=value …] --reason "…" [--wait] [--ttl <minutes>] [--json]
                                     borrow from a pool of this Mac, e.g. a simulator:
                                     acquire simulators os=26 type=iPhone --reason "UI tests" --wait
                                     match on name, type, os, udid, booted. --ttl is how long
                                     the lease lasts with no sign of you; renew starts it again
  ripul-train renew <leaseId>
  ripul-train pools [--all] [--json]  this Mac's pools: who holds what, who is waiting
  ripul-train notices [on|off]       whether a finished train tells the chats that asked for
                                     it (on by default), and who was told lately
  ripul-train block <commit> --reason "…" [--ttl <minutes>]
  ripul-train unblock <blockId|commit>
  ripul-train cancel <trainId>
  ripul-train force <trainId>        run its waiting arrival step now, over busy agents
  ripul-train status [--json]
  ripul-train config                 check the tracks and resources, repo and this Mac's
  ripul-train log [--limit N]
  ripul-train daemon                 run the daemon in the foreground
  ripul-train install | uninstall    manage the launchd agent

Inside a Ripul CLI session the caller is identified by RIPUL_CHAT_ID, so
holds are attributed to the agent that made them, and a chat that asked for
a train is told when it ends, if it is not mid-turn then (notices.mjs). A lease held
by an agent mid-turn renews itself; pools work outside a repository too.
33:- **You are told when your train ends, if you are not mid-turn then.** Ask for a train, end your turn, and a line from Trainyard arrives in your chat and starts your next turn when the train ships, fails or is cancelled. A chat that is still waiting on the train (`--wait`, which `deploy:all` uses) gets nothing more: it has the result already. See [Notices](#notices).
54:| `arrive` | Steps after the job. `when-idle: <resource>` waits until that resource is idle: for an `agents` resource (or a name not declared), until the other agents' turns end (with `include-requester`, the requester's too). The built-in action is `host-reload`, and `run:` takes any command. `max-wait-minutes` (default 30) skips the step rather than force it. |
123:When a train ends, each chat that asked for it is sent one line in its own chat, which starts that chat's next turn. Before this an agent that boarded a train and ended its turn waited for a person to say the train had arrived (11 October 2026). The code is `notices.mjs`.
126:Trainyard: the web train you asked for (train_812) has arrived. Commit a1b2c3d4e shipped. The host page has reloaded onto it.
131:- **What it says.** The track, the train, the commit and the result. A failure adds the reason and the step's log file. A cancelled train says who cancelled it. An arrival step that was skipped because other agents stayed busy is named, and for the host reload the line says the page may still be on the older build.
133:- **Only when the chat is not mid-turn.** The daemon asks the host who is mid-turn at the moment the train ends. A chat that is, is either watching the train with `--wait` or busy with something else, and is sent nothing, even if it goes idle a second later. A chat in which a turn starts before the line could be handed over is sent nothing either.
136:- **How it reaches the chat.** `host.notices.deliver` posts `trainyard_notice` to the host's `/mcp/invoke` under the chat id `trainyard`. The web app answers that call itself, before any tool lookup, and only for that chat id; it is in no agent's tool list (`chrome-extension/src/trainyard/trainNotice.ts`). It saves the line as a message from Trainyard and starts the turn with the host's own `agent:start`, the way an answered browser card continues a chat. It is not an agent message: no envelope, no reply expected, and it does not change who the turn belongs to. The host answers `delivered`, `busy`, `not-ready` (the page cannot start a turn yet), `no-chat` (the chat is not open on this host) or `failed`.
171:While a chat waits on a train, the chat shows it: a row under the tool call that boarded it, saying what the train is doing (queued behind another, held and by whom, checking, running, live but waiting to reload the host, arrived or failed) with a running clock. On iPhone and Catalyst the row is native, drawn through the same embed slot the tool lozenges ride.
176:- **Tapping the row** shows the train in full. On the web it is a dialog with every step and Arrive now (`trainyard:force`) while an arrival waits for other agents. The native row posts `ripulTrainRowOpened`, and the app presents the Trainyard screen's own train detail in a sheet (`TrainyardRowSheet` in `iOS/TrainyardScreen.swift`), with Arrive Now and Cancel Train. A queued request opens the train it waits behind.

136:- **How it reaches the chat.** `host.notices.deliver` posts `trainyard_notice` to the host's `/mcp/invoke` under the chat id `trainyard`. The web app answers that call itself, before any tool lookup, and only for that chat id; it is in no agent's tool list (`chrome-extension/src/trainyard/trainNotice.ts`). It saves the line as a message from Trainyard and starts the turn with the host's own `agent:start`, the way an answered browser card continues a chat. It is not an agent message: no envelope, no reply expected, and it does not change who the turn belongs to. The host answers `delivered`, `busy`, `not-ready` (the page cannot start a turn yet), `no-chat` (the chat is not open on this host) or `failed`.
171:While a chat waits on a train, the chat shows it: a row under the tool call that boarded it, saying what the train is doing (queued behind another, held and by whom, checking, running, live but waiting to reload the host, arrived or failed) with a running clock. On iPhone and Catalyst the row is native, drawn through the same embed slot the tool lozenges ride.
176:- **Tapping the row** shows the train in full. On the web it is a dialog with every step and Arrive now (`trainyard:force`) while an arrival waits for other agents. The native row posts `ripulTrainRowOpened`, and the app presents the Trainyard screen's own train detail in a sheet (`TrainyardRowSheet` in `iOS/TrainyardScreen.swift`), with Arrive Now and Cancel Train. A queued request opens the train it waits behind.

Level 1 is done on branch `theme`: the app now takes the website's colours with no Swift line changed, and I have stopped there as the guide requires. In dark mode three navy buttons disappear into the navy ground, so this is not ready to ship as it stands.

It is a SwiftUI iPhone app (iOS 26, XcodeGen), so the guide applies. The branch is two commits, not pushed and not merged.

## Decision for you

Which level next?
- **Stop at level 1**: light mode is presentable; dark mode has the button and list problems below.
- **Level 2 (my recommendation)**: a few lines of Swift to fix the dark-mode buttons, the two lists and the body text colour.
- **Level 3**: rewrite all 55 call sites to explicit theme accessors.

## What changed (measured)

- **Diff against `main`**: 5 files, 56 insertions, 5 deletions, 0 Swift lines.
- **`project.yml`**: SDK pin moved from 0.7.169 to 0.7.172, and the `RipulThemeRedirect` plug-in switched on.
- **`SandsendRetreats/Theme/sandsend.json`**: the theme document, the only file added. No fonts are bundled.
- **`-skipPackagePluginValidation`** added to `scripts/ship_ota.py` (the archive call), the two build commands in `CLAUDE.md`, and the one in `README.md`. I did not run the ship script.
- **`CLAUDE.md`**: a new section, "The theme".

## Where the colours came from

All from the site's Squarespace palette in its `site.css`:

| Colour | Hex | Use on the site |
|---|---|---|
| Navy | `#1C3664` | text, buttons, the navy sections' ground |
| Sand | `#E5D4C3` | text and buttons on navy |
| Shell | `#EFE5DB` | the pale sections' ground, button text on navy |
| Slate | `#535866` | the palette's dark accent |

- **Light** follows the site's white and shell sections: navy on white cards over a shell ground.
- **Dark** follows the site's navy sections: sand on navy, so the dark values are mostly the site's own.
- **Derived, not from the site**: the raised navy for cards in dark (`#27457A`), the faint text colours and the hairlines.
- **Contrast (computed)**: main text is 8.3:1 or better in both modes; secondary text is 4.4:1 at worst (dark, on a card); tertiary text is about 2.6–3.2:1, much like the system's own.

## What follows the theme and what does not (from the screenshots)

**Follows it:** page grounds, cards, the accent on icons, card headings and the tab bar, and secondary and tertiary text.

**Does not:**
- **Navy buttons in dark mode.** "Continue", "Open My Guide", "Call …" and "Find the Perfect Chef" use `Brand.navy`, which is almost the same navy as the dark ground (1.05:1). The button's shape vanishes, though its white label still reads.
- **The What's On and Dogs lists.** Their ground and rows stay the system's grey in light and black in dark, beside navy screens elsewhere.
- **Text with no colour of its own.** Body copy and large navigation titles stay black in light and white in dark. Both are readable.
- **`Brand.navy` and `Brand.cream`.** These are the app's own colours (`#24386B`, slightly different from the site's navy) and are used at 14 places, including the date badges.
- **Fonts.** The site's IvyPresto Display and Freight Sans Pro are Adobe Fonts, which may not be bundled in an app. Headings stay Apple's serif and text stays San Francisco.

## Proof nothing moved

I captured 19 screens in light and dark, twice, on a simulator I created for this ("Sandsend Theme", iPhone 17 Pro, iOS 26.4, now shut down). Two captures of the untouched app already differ on 12 of 38 screens, in the glass tab bar and toolbar buttons, and on the light welcome screen.

| Compared with the baseline | Identical | Differ |
|---|---|---|
| Plug-in on, no theme document | 27 of 38 | 11 |
| Theme document present, launched with `-ripul.theme.document system` | 23 of 38 | 15 |

- **Where they differ**: every difference is in the tab bar, a glass toolbar button, the home indicator or the Dynamic Island, plus the light welcome screen, which already differed between the two baseline sets. The island appeared in two captures and went away on a re-capture.
- **One caveat**: three light screens (Explore end aside: Chefs end, Explore, Wellness) differ by about 6,500 pixels at the home indicator. The baseline pair showed that only on a dark screen, so I am calling it system noise by reasoning, not by an exact match.
- **Release** builds, and its Stay screen matches the themed Debug one to within 47 pixels of glass, so the theme loads there.

## Other decisions

- **Font stand-in.** I asked Peter and got no answer in four minutes, so I bundled nothing. My suggestion is Playfair Display with Source Sans 3, both under the SIL Open Font Licence; Cormorant Garamond is a lighter alternative for headings.
- **Whether `Brand.navy` gives way to the theme's navy**, or stays fixed.
- **The SDK in Release.** The theme is now the one use of the SDK outside `#if DEBUG`, which bears on the open question in `CLAUDE.md` about taking the package out of Release.
- **The SDK moved three releases** (0.7.169 to 0.7.172) for the whole app, the developer console included. I did not open the console to check it.

## Not tested

A real phone, an archive or the ship script, Dynamic Type, Increased Contrast, right-to-left, and the developer console on the new SDK. Level 1 also rests on compiler behaviour (Swift 6.4, Xcode 27.1) that the language does not promise; if it changes, the cure is to switch the plug-in off.

Screenshots are in `/tmp/sandsend-theme-shots/`: `l1-theme/light` and `l1-theme/dark` for the themed app, `base1` and `base2` for the baseline, and `sheet-light-a.png`, `sheet-dark-a.png` and `sheet-dark-b.png` as contact sheets.

| Navy | `#1C3664` | text, buttons, the navy sections' ground |
| Sand | `#E5D4C3` | text and buttons on navy |
| Shell | `#EFE5DB` | the pale sections' ground, button text on navy |
| Slate | `#535866` | the palette's dark accent |

- **Light** follows the site's white and shell sections: navy on white cards over a shell ground.
- **Dark** follows the site's navy sections: sand on navy, so the dark values are mostly the site's own.
- **Derived, not from the site**: the raised navy for cards in dark (`#27457A`), the faint text colours and the hairlines.
- **Contrast (computed)**: main text is 8.3:1 or better in both modes; secondary text is 4.4:1 at worst (dark, on a card); tertiary text is about 2.6–3.2:1, much like the system's own.

## What follows the theme and what does not (from the screenshots)

**Follows it:** page grounds, cards, the accent on icons, card headings and the tab bar, and secondary and tertiary text.

**Does not:**
- **Navy buttons in dark mode.** "Continue", "Open My Guide", "Call …" and "Find the Perfect Chef" use `Brand.navy`, which is almost the same navy as the dark ground (1.05:1). The button's shape vanishes, though its white label still reads.
- **The What's On and Dogs lists.** Their ground and rows stay the system's grey in light and black in dark, beside navy screens elsewhere.
- **Text with no colour of its own.** Body copy and large navigation titles stay black in light and white in dark. Both are readable.
- **`Brand.navy` and `Brand.cream`.** These are the app's own colours (`#24386B`, slightly different from the site's navy) and are used at 14 places, including the date badges.
- **Fonts.** The site's IvyPresto Display and Freight Sans Pro are Adobe Fonts, which may not be bundled in an app. Headings stay Apple's serif and text stays San Francisco.

## Proof nothing moved

I captured 19 screens in light and dark, twice, on a simulator I created for this ("Sandsend Theme", iPhone 17 Pro, iOS 26.4, now shut down). Two captures of the untouched app already differ on 12 of 38 screens, in the glass tab bar and toolbar buttons, and on the light welcome screen.

| Compared with the baseline | Identical | Differ |
|---|---|---|
| Plug-in on, no theme document | 27 of 38 | 11 |
| Theme document present, launched with `-ripul.theme.document system` | 23 of 38 | 15 |

- **Where they differ**: every difference is in the tab bar, a glass toolbar button, the home indicator or the Dynamic Island, plus the light welcome screen, which already differed between the two baseline sets. The island appeared in two captures and went away on a re-capture.
- **One caveat**: three light screens (Explore end aside: Chefs end, Explore, Wellness) differ by about 6,500 pixels at the home indicator. The baseline pair showed that only on a dark screen, so I am calling it system noise by reasoning, not by an exact match.
- **Release** builds, and its Stay screen matches the themed Debug one to within 47 pixels of glass, so the theme loads there.

## Other decisions

- **Font stand-in.** I asked Peter and got no answer in four minutes, so I bundled nothing. My suggestion is Playfair Display with Source Sans 3, both under the SIL Open Font Licence; Cormorant Garamond is a lighter alternative for headings.
- **Whether `Brand.navy` gives way to the theme's navy**, or stays fixed.
- **The SDK in Release.** The theme is now the one use of the SDK outside `#if DEBUG`, which bears on the open question in `CLAUDE.md` about taking the package out of Release.
- **The SDK moved three releases** (0.7.169 to 0.7.172) for the whole app, the developer console included. I did not open the console to check it.

## Not tested

A real phone, an archive or the ship script, Dynamic Type, Increased Contrast, right-to-left, and the developer console on the new SDK. Level 1 also rests on compiler behaviour (Swift 6.4, Xcode 27.1) that the language does not promise; if it changes, the cure is to switch the plug-in off.

Screenshots are in `/tmp/sandsend-theme-shots/`: `l1-theme/light` and `l1-theme/dark` for the themed app, `base1` and `base2` for the baseline, and `sheet-light-a.png`, `sheet-dark-a.png` and `sheet-dark-b.png` as contact sheets.

cd /Users/petermaude/Documents/ripul && cat >> docs/plans/sdk-theme-host-burden.md <<'EOF'

## Fourth trial: from the starting prompt, on the released SDK

- **It works from one tap.** An agent given only the starter's words and the website's address read the `theming` guide three seconds in, and 27 minutes later Sandsend was on the website's colours with not one line of Swift changed (measured: `git diff main` is 5 files, 56 lines added, 5 removed, no `.swift` file).
- **The trust step did not stop it.** It never met the failure: the guide named the flag, so its first build with the plug-in from the released package already carried `-skipPackagePluginValidation` and succeeded. It then wrote the flag into the ship script, the README and the app's CLAUDE.md unasked.
- **What it did not deliver: the fonts, and a dark mode fit to ship.** It asked a person which stand-in font to use, nobody answered in four minutes, and it bundled none. Three navy buttons vanish on the navy dark ground. Both are faults of the guide, and both are fixed in it.

Sandsend Retreats, a clean copy of `main` at `030186d` in `/tmp/sandsend-starter`, branch `theme` (commits `01fb9b7` and `3a7a51f`, not pushed). The public package at v0.7.172 and web build `mv3qz97a`. 11 October 2026, 12:36:53 to 13:04:25. The agent was a new Claude chat ("Sandsend: theme it from the starter") whose whole task was the text the starter "Start with no change to the source" puts in the composer, and one sentence: "The look to follow is the app's website, www.sandsendretreats.com." Everything below is measured from its branch, its files and its transcript, not from its reply, except where marked.

### What it did, by the clock

| Clock | What | Measured from |
|---|---|---|
| 12:36:53 | Started. | the spawn call |
| 12:36:58 | Read the `theming` guide. Then `trains`, `session` and `devices`. | transcript |
| 12:37:05 | Made the branch `theme`. Read the app's theme file, routes and project file. | transcript, git |
| 12:38:16 | Cloned the public package to `/tmp` for the tools, as the guide says. Ran `migrate --dry-run --named` (55 lines) and counted by search what no level reaches. | transcript |
| 12:38:30 | Fetched the website's stylesheet and six of its pages. | transcript |
| 12:39 to 12:46 | Built the untouched app, made a simulator of its own, captured 19 screens in light and dark, twice. | transcript |
| 12:42:20 | Asked a person which stand-in to use for the site's two Adobe fonts, with three choices. No answer; the question lapsed at 12:46:51. | transcript |
| 12:47:07 | Moved the pin from 0.7.169 to 0.7.172 and switched the plug-in on: 7 lines of `project.yml`, 4 of them a comment. | git |
| 12:48:36 | First build with the plug-in: succeeded, with the flag. | transcript |
| 12:52 to 12:55 | Compared the plug-in build, with no document, against both baseline sets. One new difference, on the Story screen: the Dynamic Island had appeared in a capture. Captured again; gone. | transcript |
| 12:55:01 | First commit. Wrote the theme document from the site's palette and built. | git |
| 12:55 to 13:03 | Captured the themed app, and the themed build launched with `-ripul.theme.document system`. Built Release. | transcript |
| 13:04:00 | Second commit. Stopped and asked which level next, as the guide requires. | git, transcript |

64 tool calls. Of the 27.5 minutes, about 4.5 were waiting for a person and about 12 were builds and screenshot passes (my estimate from the marks above).

### Against the third trial

| | Third trial (an agent that had built the plug-in) | Fourth (a customer's agent, the starter only) |
|---|---|---|
| Swift lines changed | 0 | 0 |
| Diff | 230 lines in 9 files, 199 of them font licences and a note | 56 added, 5 removed, in 5 files |
| Project settings | 3 lines | 3 lines, and 4 of comment |
| Theme document | 28 lines, copied from the second trial | 33 lines, written from the website's own stylesheet |
| Fonts | 4 files, copied from the second trial | none: see below |
| Package | a local path, so no trust step | released v0.7.172, with the flag from the first build |
| The flag written into the repository's commands | not needed | the ship script, the README and two commands in CLAUDE.md |
| Screens compared under the system look | 36, baseline captured once | 38, baseline captured twice |
| Time | about two hours, most of it building the plug-in | 27.5 minutes |

### The five questions

1. **Did it find and read the guide?** Yes, first, before it looked at any file. The starter's words name it.
2. **Did it reach a themed app with no Swift changed?** Yes. I opened its contact sheets: paper and navy in light, navy and sand in dark, the cards, the accent and the tab bar all follow. Body text is black in light and white in dark, and the two lists are the system's, as level 1 leaves them. It said so and named the screens.
3. **Did it meet the trust step and get past it?** It got past it without meeting it. Separately, before the release, I measured the failure itself on a versioned copy of the package: without the flag the build stops with `Validate plug-in “RipulThemeRedirect” in package “…”` and no other explanation; with it the build succeeds. In Xcode's own window the step is a prompt, which was not tested.
4. **Did anything in the guide mislead it?** Three things, below.
5. **Did it prove nothing moved?** Mostly. Of 38 screens, 27 matched the baseline exactly with the plug-in on and no document, and 23 with the document present and the system look asked for. Every difference was in the tab bar, a glass toolbar button, the home indicator or the Dynamic Island, and none in the app's own content. For three light screens it could not match the difference to one in its baseline pair, and called it the system's by reasoning; it said so.

### What misled it, and what I changed

Each change is in the skill file and so in the guide, which is the same text.

1. **Fonts.** The guide said to propose a stand-in and "let the person decide". It asked, nobody answered, and it bundled nothing, so the most visible part of the brand is missing. Now: ask once, and if no answer comes, bundle the proposed open-licence font in a commit of its own, so it can be dropped, and list it as a decision still open.
2. **How much two captures differ.** The guide said a glass control differs "by a thousand or so pixels". On this run 12 of 38 screens differed between two captures of the untouched app: the tab bar, toolbar buttons, the home indicator, the Dynamic Island. It spent about three minutes on the Story screen before capturing it again. Now the guide says which parts differ, says to record where each difference is and not only whether there is one, and says to capture again before believing a new difference in the status bar or tab bar.
3. **The app's own colours against the theme's ground.** The guide warned about text contrast and said nothing of the app's fixed colours. The agent chose the site's navy for the dark ground, and the app's own navy buttons, which level 1 cannot reach, vanished on it. It caught this in its screenshots and reported it, but only after choosing. Now the guide says to check those colours against the grounds in both modes before settling the values.

Also added: a Mac has no image library, so the guide now says to make a virtual environment with Pillow (the agent found this out and did so, one minute).

Not the guide's: one `ripul_guide` call timed out while the host reloaded, and one search failed on the shell's handling of `*`.

### What I would still not claim

- **A person in Xcode.** The trust prompt, and adding the plug-in by clicking.
- **A project with no generator.** Sandsend uses XcodeGen. The guide tells an agent to ask the person to add the plug-in in Xcode otherwise; not tried.
- **A second agent, or Codex.** One run, one harness.
- **Levels 2 and 3 from a starter.** This run stopped at the question, as it should.
- **That a person would have tapped this row.** The row is in the build; nobody but me has seen it.

### On the phone

**Built and signed, and waiting for the phone.** The trial's branch at `3a7a51f` is at `/tmp/sandsend-starter-device.app` (measured: `BUILD SUCCEEDED`, team C7AA358R56, the theme document in the bundle). Peter's iPhone has been unreachable from the Mac Studio since 10:40, by CoreDevice and by the bridge, and still was at 13:06. `/tmp/sandsend-starter-install.sh` checks each minute for four hours and installs and launches the build when the phone answers; its log is beside it. It replaced the job that was waiting to install the third trial's build. The app opens on the theme with no argument, because the theme is the bundle's only document. It has the website's colours and the system's fonts.
EOF
A=(docs/plans/sdk-theme-host-burden.md ripul-ios-sdk/tools/skills/theme-an-app/SKILL.md chrome-extension/public/guides/theming.md); git add $A && git commit -q -m "Theming: the fourth trial, from the starting prompt on the released SDK, and what it changed in the guide

A customer's agent given only the starter's words themed Sandsend with no Swift changed in
27 minutes. The guide and skill now say what to do when nobody answers about a font, how
much two captures of one build differ, and to check the app's own colours against the
theme's ground.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>" -- $A && git push -q; git log --oneline -1; git status -sb | head -3

64 tool calls. Of the 27.5 minutes, about 4.5 were waiting for a person and about 12 were builds and screenshot passes (my estimate from the marks above).

### Against the third trial

| | Third trial (an agent that had built the plug-in) | Fourth (a customer's agent, the starter only) |
|---|---|---|
| Swift lines changed | 0 | 0 |
| Diff | 230 lines in 9 files, 199 of them font licences and a note | 56 added, 5 removed, in 5 files |
| Project settings | 3 lines | 3 lines, and 4 of comment |
| Theme document | 28 lines, copied from the second trial | 33 lines, written from the website's own stylesheet |
| Fonts | 4 files, copied from the second trial | none: see below |
| Package | a local path, so no trust step | released v0.7.172, with the flag from the first build |
| The flag written into the repository's commands | not needed | the ship script, the README and two commands in CLAUDE.md |
| Screens compared under the system look | 36, baseline captured once | 38, baseline captured twice |
| Time | about two hours, most of it building the plug-in | 27.5 minutes |

### The five questions

1. **Did it find and read the guide?** Yes, first, before it looked at any file. The starter's words name it.
2. **Did it reach a themed app with no Swift changed?** Yes. I opened its contact sheets: paper and navy in light, navy and sand in dark, the cards, the accent and the tab bar all follow. Body text is black in light and white in dark, and the two lists are the system's, as level 1 leaves them. It said so and named the screens.
3. **Did it meet the trust step and get past it?** It got past it without meeting it. Separately, before the release, I measured the failure itself on a versioned copy of the package: without the flag the build stops with `Validate plug-in “RipulThemeRedirect” in package “…”` and no other explanation; with it the build succeeds. In Xcode's own window the step is a prompt, which was not tested.
4. **Did anything in the guide mislead it?** Three things, below.
5. **Did it prove nothing moved?** Mostly. Of 38 screens, 27 matched the baseline exactly with the plug-in on and no document, and 23 with the document present and the system look asked for. Every difference was in the tab bar, a glass toolbar button, the home indicator or the Dynamic Island, and none in the app's own content. For three light screens it could not match the difference to one in its baseline pair, and called it the system's by reasoning; it said so.

### What misled it, and what I changed

Each change is in the skill file and so in the guide, which is the same text.

1. **Fonts.** The guide said to propose a stand-in and "let the person decide". It asked, nobody answered, and it bundled nothing, so the most visible part of the brand is missing. Now: ask once, and if no answer comes, bundle the proposed open-licence font in a commit of its own, so it can be dropped, and list it as a decision still open.
2. **How much two captures differ.** The guide said a glass control differs "by a thousand or so pixels". On this run 12 of 38 screens differed between two captures of the untouched app: the tab bar, toolbar buttons, the home indicator, the Dynamic Island. It spent about three minutes on the Story screen before capturing it again. Now the guide says which parts differ, says to record where each difference is and not only whether there is one, and says to capture again before believing a new difference in the status bar or tab bar.
3. **The app's own colours against the theme's ground.** The guide warned about text contrast and said nothing of the app's fixed colours. The agent chose the site's navy for the dark ground, and the app's own navy buttons, which level 1 cannot reach, vanished on it. It caught this in its screenshots and reported it, but only after choosing. Now the guide says to check those colours against the grounds in both modes before settling the values.

Also added: a Mac has no image library, so the guide now says to make a virtual environment with Pillow (the agent found this out and did so, one minute).

Not the guide's: one `ripul_guide` call timed out while the host reloaded, and one search failed on the shell's handling of `*`.

### What I would still not claim

- **A person in Xcode.** The trust prompt, and adding the plug-in by clicking.
- **A project with no generator.** Sandsend uses XcodeGen. The guide tells an agent to ask the person to add the plug-in in Xcode otherwise; not tried.
- **A second agent, or Codex.** One run, one harness.
- **Levels 2 and 3 from a starter.** This run stopped at the question, as it should.
- **That a person would have tapped this row.** The row is in the build; nobody but me has seen it.

### On the phone

**Built and signed, and waiting for the phone.** The trial's branch at `3a7a51f` is at `/tmp/sandsend-starter-device.app` (measured: `BUILD SUCCEEDED`, team C7AA358R56, the theme document in the bundle). Peter's iPhone has been unreachable from the Mac Studio since 10:40, by CoreDevice and by the bridge, and still was at 13:06. `/tmp/sandsend-starter-install.sh` checks each minute for four hours and installs and launches the build when the phone answers; its log is beside it. It replaced the job that was waiting to install the third trial's build. The app opens on the theme with no argument, because the theme is the bundle's only document. It has the website's colours and the system's fonts.
